procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Sessions Judge, at Moradabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 25, 1955, of the Allahabad High Court, in Criminal Appeal No. 702 of 1955 and Referred No. 77 of 1955 arising out of the judgment and order dated May 17, 1955, of the Court of Sessions Judge, at Moradabad in Sessions Trial No. 29 of 1955.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant appealed to the High Court of Allahabad, but his appeal was dismissed and the conviction and sentence was affirmed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant obtained special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against the decision of the Allahabad High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the opinion of a fire-arms expert can be considered conclusive proof that a specific cartridge was fired from a particular pistol.

facts: A cartridge (Ex. I) was found at the scene of a murder.
The appellant later produced a pistol (Ex. III) from a concealed location.
A fire-arms expert was tasked with determining if the cartridge was fired from the appellant's pistol.
The expert fired four test cartridges from the pistol and compared the markings on them with the evidence cartridge (Ex. I).
He found that "exactly identical markings" and "individual characteristics" from the pistol's chamber were present on both the test cartridges and the evidence cartridge.
The expert provided microphotographs to support his findings.
law: The court accepted the scientific principle that every firearm has unique, individual characteristics on its breech face, striking pin, and chamber.
When a cartridge is fired, the immense pressure impresses these unique markings onto the softer material of the cartridge case.
By comparing an evidence cartridge with a test-fired cartridge from a specific firearm under a microscope, a definite identification can be made if the marks are clear.

The court also consulted authoritative texts on crime investigation (by Kirk, and Soderman and O'Connel) which confirmed that cartridge cases carry distinctive markings that can be used for positive identification of the firearm.
application: The court found that the expert had conducted the necessary scientific tests carefully and saw "no good reason for distrusting his opinion."
It noted that the expert's opinion had not been challenged during cross-examination.
The judges of the High Court had also examined the microphotographs and were satisfied with the expert's evidence.
To further ensure there was no error, the Supreme Court itself reviewed works by leading authors on the subject, which validated the expert's methodology and the reliability of such evidence.
The court determined that since the expert's process was sound and his conclusions were based on established scientific principles, it was safe to accept his opinion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the opinion of the fire-arms expert conclusively proved that the specific cartridge (Ex. I) was fired from the particular pistol (Ex. III). This conclusion was based on the expert's careful scientific testing, the unchallenged nature of his testimony, and the validation of his methods by authoritative texts on the subject.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Election Tribunal is justified in setting aside an entire election for a double-seat constituency when the result has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a single nomination paper.

facts: The case involved an election for a double-seat constituency.
An Election Tribunal found that the result of the election had been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper.
The Supreme Court viewed the election for a double-seat constituency as 'one integral whole'.
law: The Court cited Section 100 of the relevant statute, which mandates that if an Election Tribunal finds that the result of an election has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper, 'the Tribunal shall declare the election to be wholly void'.
application: The Court applied the clear language of Section 100 to the facts.
Since the Tribunal had found that the improper rejection materially affected the election result, the law required the election to be declared 'wholly void'.
Because the election for the double-seat constituency was considered a single, 'integral whole', a declaration that it was 'wholly void' meant the entire election had to be set aside.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Election Tribunal was justified in setting aside the election as a whole.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party can lose their right to a property through adverse possession during the pendency of a related suit.

facts: A court-appointed Receiver took possession of the properties in February 1928 during the pendency of a suit filed by H.
After the suit was decreed, H obtained possession from the Receiver on January 20, 1930.
The respondent filed the present suit for his share of the property on October 23, 1941.
The appellant (H's successor) argued that the time the Receiver was in possession should be added to the time H was in possession to meet the requirement for adverse possession.
law: The possession of a property by a court-appointed Receiver during a pending suit (pendente lite) is not considered adverse to any party.
Such possession cannot be added to or "tacked" onto a party's subsequent period of possession for the purpose of calculating the time for adverse possession.
application: The court first assumed, for the sake of argument, that H's possession from January 20, 1930, was adverse to the respondent.
It found that this period alone (from 1930 to 1941) was not long enough to displace the respondent's title.
The court then ruled that the prior period when the Receiver was in possession could not be added to H's period of possession to meet the statutory time requirement.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the respondent did not lose his right to the property through adverse possession because the period during which the court's Receiver was in possession could not be counted towards the appellant's claim.

issue.issue_text: Whether the period during which a property is in the possession of a Receiver can be counted towards establishing a claim of adverse possession.

facts: A person 'H' filed a suit to recover properties belonging to a deceased relative 'V'.
During the lawsuit, a Receiver was appointed to take possession of the properties in February 1928.
After the suit was decreed in his favor, H obtained possession of the properties from the Receiver on January 20, 1930.
H's heir, the appellant, later took possession.
In 1941, the respondent, another co-heir, sued for his share of the properties.
The appellant defended the suit by claiming adverse possession, arguing that the time the Receiver held the property should be added to the time H and the appellant held it.
law: The period during which a court-appointed Receiver is in possession of a property cannot be added or 'tacked' to a subsequent period of personal possession for the purpose of establishing a claim of adverse possession.
application: The Court analyzed the appellant's claim for adverse possession.
It considered the period starting from when H took actual possession from the Receiver (January 20, 1930) until the respondent filed the current suit (October 23, 1941).
The Court explicitly refused to add the prior period (from February 1928 to January 1930) when the Receiver was in possession.
It determined that H's possession, even if considered adverse, was 'not adequate in time' on its own to displace the respondent's title.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the period during which the Receiver was in possession could not be counted towards establishing a claim of adverse possession. Consequently, the appellant's claim failed as the required time period for adverse possession was not met.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the opinion of a fire-arms expert can be considered conclusive proof that a specific cartridge was fired from a particular pistol.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued against the circumstantial evidence, suggesting the pistol was planted in his house by someone else, thus making the expert's opinion linking the pistol to the crime scene irrelevant.
respondent_arguments: The fire-arms expert's opinion, based on scientific tests showing identical markings on the evidence cartridge and test cartridges fired from the pistol, conclusively proved the link between the weapon and the crime scene.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Election Tribunal is justified in setting aside an entire election for a double-seat constituency when the result has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a single nomination paper.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that setting aside the entire election for a double-seat constituency was an excessive measure for the improper rejection of a single nomination paper.
respondent_arguments: Section 100 of the relevant act mandates that the election shall be declared 'wholly void' if the result was materially affected. Furthermore, an election for a double-seat constituency is considered 'one integral whole' and cannot be partially voided.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a party can lose their right to a property through adverse possession during the pendency of a related suit.
appellant_arguments: The appellant claimed that the period during which a suit regarding the property was pending should be counted towards establishing their claim of adverse possession.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that they did not lose their right to the property, as the period during which a suit is pending cannot be counted towards a claim of adverse possession.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the period during which a property is in the possession of a Receiver can be counted towards establishing a claim of adverse possession.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's claim for adverse possession implicitly required that the time the property was held by a court-appointed Receiver be counted in their favor.
respondent_arguments: The period a property is held by a Receiver cannot be counted towards adverse possession, as the Receiver's possession is legally the possession of the court and is not adverse to the rightful owner.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If the result of an election for a double-seat constituency has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper, the election must be declared wholly void, as such an election is considered one integral whole.
obiter: The opinion of a fire-arms expert can conclusively prove that a specific cartridge was fired from a particular pistol.
Circumstantial evidence can be sufficient to establish the guilt of an appellant.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court reached three distinct conclusions based on the provided text. First, in a criminal matter, it held that the opinion of a fire-arms expert can be conclusive proof linking a specific weapon to a crime, and that this, combined with other circumstantial evidence such as motive and the accused's actions, is sufficient to uphold a conviction. Second, in an election dispute, the court affirmed that under the relevant statute, an election for a double-seat constituency is an 'integral whole' and must be declared 'wholly void' if the result was materially affected by a single improper nomination rejection. Third, in a property dispute, the court ruled that a party cannot lose their property rights through adverse possession during the pendency of a related suit, which implicitly includes any period the property is held by a court-appointed Receiver.
legal_tests_applied: In the election matter, the court applied Section 100 of the relevant act, which provides that if a Tribunal finds the result of an election has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper, 'the Tribunal shall declare the election to be wholly void'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument in the criminal case, that the pistol was planted, was rejected because the court found no reason to disbelieve the witnesses who saw the appellant produce the pistol from a corn-bin inside his house, with circumstances indicating that 'no one but the appellant could have' hidden it there.

In the election case, the appellant's contention failed because the court found the Tribunal was justified in setting aside the election as a whole, as the election for a double-seat constituency was 'one integral whole' and the statute mandated it be declared 'wholly void'.
The appellant's claim of adverse possession failed because the court held that the respondent 'did not lose his right by adverse possession during the pendency of H's suit'.

The appellant's claim to count the period a Receiver held the property towards adverse possession failed because the court's primary ruling—that time does not run during a pending suit—necessarily excludes the period of possession by a court-appointed Receiver during that suit.
why_respondent_won: In the criminal case, the respondent's position was upheld because the court held that 'the opinion of the fire-arms expert conclusively proved that the cartridge Ex. I had been fired from the pistol Ex. III', and this, along with other circumstantial evidence, was 'sufficient to establish the guilt of the appellant'.

In the election matter, the respondent prevailed because the court agreed that Section 100 of the act required the election to be declared 'wholly void' and that the election for a double-seat constituency was 'one integral whole', justifying the setting aside of the entire election.
The respondent in the property dispute succeeded because the court explicitly held that the respondent 'did not lose his right by adverse possession during the pendency of H's suit'.
